ADVANCEMENTS AGAINST AN INTESTATE SHARE (PROB. CODE § 6409) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Taylor Morgan

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes a single California statutory rule, Probate Code § 6409, governing when a lifetime gift from Pat Morgan to an heir, such as Taylor Morgan, is treated as an "advancement" -- a credit against that heir's share of an intestate estate (an estate, or the part of an estate, that passes because there is no valid will covering it). It states facts about California law generally. It does not determine whether any specific lifetime gift Pat Morgan made was or was not an advancement, and it does not advise on what to do about a particular gift or asset.

A LIFETIME GIFT IS NOT AN ADVANCEMENT UNLESS A WRITING SAYS SO
California's advancement statute applies only when a person dies intestate as to all or part of their estate. Property the decedent gave during their lifetime to an heir is treated as an advancement against that heir's share of the intestate estate only if one of two conditions is met: either the decedent declared in a contemporaneous writing that the gift was an advancement against the heir's share (or that its value was to be deducted from that share), or the heir acknowledged in writing that the gift was to be so deducted or was an advancement. The mere fact that a lifetime gift was made, without such a writing, does not by itself make the gift an advancement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "(a) If a person dies intestate as to all or part of his or her estate, property the decedent gave during lifetime to an heir is treated as an advancement against that heir’s share of the intestate estate only if one of the following conditions is satisfied: (1) The decedent declares in a contemporaneous writing that the gift is an advancement against the heir’s share of the estate or that its value is to be deducted from the value of the heir’s share of the estate. (2) The heir acknowledges in writing that the gift is to be so deducted or is an advancement or that its value is to be deducted from the value of the heir’s share of the estate."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 6409(a), Cal. Prob. Code § 6409(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6409.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of an actual, sourced writing requirement -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, and not a claim that any particular lifetime gift meets or fails this test. Some states apply a common-law presumption that a substantial lifetime gift to a child is an advancement absent contrary evidence; this statute instead requires an affirmative contemporaneous writing from one side or the other before any lifetime gift is treated as an advancement at all -- but this document does not independently verify what rule, if any, applies in a state other than California. This clause combines subdivision (a) and its two numbered conditions, (a)(1) and (a)(2), which are all part of the same statutory subdivision; no additional independent source was found for this.

WHEN AN ADVANCED GIFT'S VALUE IS MEASURED
Once a lifetime gift qualifies as an advancement, a default timing rule fixes when its value is measured for purposes of crediting it against the heir's intestate share: the property advanced is valued as of the time the heir came into possession or enjoyment of the property, or as of the time of the decedent's death, whichever occurs first. This default is subject to a separate rule that can fix the value differently when a contemporaneous writing itself states a value.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "(b) Subject to subdivision (c), the property advanced is to be valued as of the time the heir came into possession or enjoyment of the property or as of the time of death of the decedent, whichever occurs first."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 6409(b), Cal. Prob. Code § 6409(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6409.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of an actual default valuation-timing rule -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific advancement, and not a claim about how any particular piece of advanced property should be valued. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 6409(b)); no additional independent source was found for this.

A VALUE STATED IN THE WRITING ITSELF CONTROLS
The default valuation-timing rule above yields to a stated value where one exists: if the value of the property advanced is expressed in the decedent's own contemporaneous writing, or in an acknowledgment the heir made contemporaneously with the advancement, that stated value is conclusive in the division and distribution of the intestate estate -- it is not displaced by evidence of the property's value at possession, enjoyment, or death.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "(c) If the value of the property advanced is expressed in the contemporaneous writing of the decedent, or in an acknowledgment of the heir made contemporaneously with the advancement, that value is conclusive in the division and distribution of the intestate estate."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 6409(c), Cal. Prob. Code § 6409(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6409.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of an actual conclusive-valuation rule -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific advancement, and not a claim about the value of any particular advanced property. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 6409(c)); no additional independent source was found for this.

IF THE HEIR WHO RECEIVED THE ADVANCEMENT PREDECEASES THE DECEDENT
A separate default rule addresses what happens to an advancement's effect if the heir who received it does not survive the decedent: if the recipient of the property advanced fails to survive the decedent, the property is not taken into account in computing the intestate share to be received by the recipient's issue (the recipient's own descendants, who may inherit in the recipient's place). That default can be overridden: the statute makes it apply "unless the declaration or acknowledgment provides otherwise," so the decedent's contemporaneous writing, or the heir's contemporaneous acknowledgment, can instead specify that the advancement carries over to the recipient's issue.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "(d) If the recipient of the property advanced fails to survive the decedent, the property is not taken into account in computing the intestate share to be received by the recipient’s issue unless the declaration or acknowledgment provides otherwise."
  — Cal. Probate Code § 6409(d), Cal. Prob. Code § 6409(d) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6409.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of an actual default rule for a predeceased recipient, and of a genuine override mechanism tied to the same writing that created the advancement in the first place -- not a claim about which state's law governs a specific estate, and not a claim about how any particular advancement's governing writing is or is not worded. This is a single statutory subdivision (§ 6409(d)); no additional independent source was found for this.

CERTIFICATION OF UNDERSTANDING
I certify that I have read this information sheet on California's statutory advancement rule (Probate Code § 6409), and that this sheet states facts about the law generally rather than advising me on whether any specific lifetime gift Pat Morgan made to Taylor Morgan is an advancement or on what to do about my own situation.

Signed: _______________________ Date: September 9, 2026
At: Sacramento, California
